questions.prompt: A sequence of errors \(e_k \to 0\) converges linearly when the successive ratios \(e_{k+1}/e_k\) tend to a limit \(\mu\) with
questions.explanation: Linear convergence means the error shrinks by a factor that settles strictly between 0 and 1. A limit above 1 would make the error grow. A limit of 0 is superlinear, which is faster than linear. A limit of 1, with the error still going to 0, is the sublinear pattern of sequences such as \(1/k\).

questions.prompt: Three successive errors are \(0.9\), \(0.45\), and \(0.225\). What is the constant successive ratio \(e_{k+1}/e_k\)?
questions.explanation: Divide \(0.45\) by \(0.9\), or \(0.225\) by \(0.45\). Both quotients are \(1/2\). The sequence is linear with rate \(1/2\). Reporting \(2\) inverts the ratio. Reporting \(0.225\) repeats the last error. Reporting \(0.9\) repeats the first.

questions.prompt: The errors \(e_k = 1/k\) for \(k \ge 1\) go to zero. Their convergence is
questions.explanation: The ratio \((1/(k+1))/(1/k) = k/(k+1)\) tends to 1. The errors go to zero, but not by a factor bounded below 1, so the rate is sublinear. Decreasing at every step is not enough for a linear rate. Superlinear convergence requires the ratio to tend to 0. A rational formula is not the definition of a quadratic rate.
options: quadratic, because the errors are a rational function of \(k\)
linear, because they decrease at every step
superlinear, because they have no constant factor
sublinear, because the successive ratios tend to 1

questions.prompt: Put these checks in the order you would apply them to a positive error sequence that tends to zero and might be linear, superlinear, or quadratic. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: A rate is a statement about an error that tends to zero, so that check comes first. The successive ratios are the next measurement, and a limit strictly inside \((0, 1)\) already classifies the sequence as linear. Only a ratio limit of 0 opens the superlinear case, and the square in the denominator is the further test that separates quadratic from merely superlinear. Squaring before the successive ratios are known skips the linear case.
steps: Confirm that the errors tend to zero.
Form the successive ratios of one error over the previous error.
If those ratios tend to a limit strictly between 0 and 1, classify the rate as linear and stop.
Only when that linear classification does not apply, because the ratios tend to 0, form the ratios of one error over the square of the previous error.
If the ratios against the square stay bounded, classify the rate as quadratic.

questions.prompt: Which of these positive sequences converge to zero superlinearly?
questions.explanation:
Superlinear convergence means the successive ratio tends to 0.
• \((1/2)^{k^2}\) has ratio \((1/2)^{2k+1}\), which tends to 0.
• \(1/k!\) has ratio \(1/(k+1)\), which tends to 0.
• \((1/2)^k\) has ratio \(1/2\), a linear rate.
• \(1/k\) has ratio tending to 1, a sublinear rate.
• \((9/10)^k\) has ratio \(9/10\), also linear.

questions.prompt: The errors obey \(e_{k+1} = c\, e_k\) with \(0 < c < 1\), and \(e_0 = a\). The error \(e_3\) equals
questions.explanation: Apply the recurrence three times: \(e_1 = c a\), \(e_2 = c^2 a\), and \(e_3 = c^3 a\). Both names are required. The product \(a \cdot c\) is only \(e_1\). The power \(c^3\) drops the starting error. The power \(a^3 c\) swaps the roles of the starting error and the rate.

questions.prompt: A note classifies the errors \(1\), \(1/2\), \(1/4\), \(1/8\), and so on. Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: Halving at every step sends the errors to 0, and the ratio is the constant \(1/2\), which lies in \((0, 1)\). That is linear convergence. It is not quadratic. The quadratic test looks at \(e_{k+1}/e_k^2 = (1/2)/e_k\), and that quantity grows without bound as the error shrinks. A bounded quadratic ratio would have to stay finite.
steps: The errors are positive and tend to 0.
A constant ratio strictly between 0 and 1 means the convergence is linear.
That same constant ratio means the convergence is quadratic.
reasons: The ratio against the square of the error is unbounded, so the rate is not quadratic.
A constant ratio in \((0, 1)\) is superlinear rather than linear.

questions.prompt: The errors begin \(1/2\), \(1/4\), \(1/16\). This is the start of \(e_{k+1} = e_k^2\). What is \(e_2 / e_1^2\)?
questions.explanation: Index them as \(e_0 = 1/2\), \(e_1 = 1/4\), \(e_2 = 1/16\). Then \(e_1^2 = 1/16\), and the ratio is \(1\). The same value is \(e_1 / e_0^2\). A quadratic rate allows this ratio to stay bounded. Here it equals 1 at every step. Reporting \(1/4\) is the successive ratio \(e_2/e_1\), which is the superlinear test rather than the quadratic one. Reporting \(1/16\) repeats \(e_2\).

questions.prompt: On a plot of \(\log e_k\) against the iteration index, linear convergence looks like
questions.explanation: If \(e_{k+1} = \mu e_k\) with \(0 < \mu < 1\), then \(\log e_k = \log e_0 + k \log \mu\). The slope \(\log \mu\) is negative, so the plot is a descending straight line. A horizontal line would be a constant error. A positive slope would be growth. A single vertical drop is not the picture of a constant factor applied at every iteration.
options: a horizontal line
a straight line with negative slope
a curve that becomes vertical in a single step and then stops
a straight line with positive slope

questions.prompt: Quadratic convergence of an error sequence implies
questions.explanation: A bounded ratio \(e_{k+1}/e_k^2\) forces \(e_{k+1}/e_k = O(e_k)\) to tend to 0 whenever the error tends to 0. Quadratic convergence is therefore superlinear. A successive-ratio limit in \((0, 1)\) is linear and is strictly slower. An arithmetic progression of errors does not go to zero unless the common difference is zero.
options: the successive ratios tend to 0, so the convergence is also superlinear
the successive ratios tend to a limit in \((0, 1)\), and no faster
the errors are bounded away from zero
the errors form an arithmetic progression

questions.prompt: Two successive errors are \(0.05\) and \(0.01\), and the same ratio continues. What is \(e_{k+1}/e_k\)?
questions.explanation: Divide \(0.01\) by \(0.05\). The quotient is \(1/5 = 0.2\). That constant in \((0, 1)\) is a linear rate. Reporting \(5\) inverts the ratio. Reporting \(0.04\) is the difference of the two errors. Reporting \(0.01\) repeats the later error.

questions.prompt: For a smooth objective that is bounded below, the general gradient method is described by a sublinear guarantee. That name means
questions.explanation: A \(1/k\) bound on the smallest squared gradient norm goes to zero, and the ratio of successive bounds tends to 1. That is sublinear. Squaring the error every iteration would be a quadratic rate, which this general guarantee does not give. One-step termination is finite convergence. A factor greater than 1 is divergence.
options: the error is squared at every iteration
the iterates reach the minimizer in one step
the successive errors grow by a factor greater than 1
the best squared gradient norm seen so far decays like \(1/k\), slower than a fixed factor each step
